lessons.title: Linguistic diversity and dialects
lessons.anelcac: Notions of linguistic diversity, dialects, names of languages, geographical classification
objectives: Becoming aware of the linguistic diversity of Cameroon (about 280 languages according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas)
Distinguish language, dialect and variant according to academic definitions
Naming Tupuri and locating it in the geographical classification of the languages of Cameroon
Adopt an attitude of respect towards all languages

teacher.intro: Lesson: Linguistic diversity and dialects. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Display the map of the Linguistic Mini-Atlas of Cameroon. Ask students which languages are spoken in their family.
**Exploration:** Have students read the definitions in the Mini-Atlas (language, dialect, patois, national language). Locate Tupuri in its linguistic region.
**Conceptualisation:** Explain the language / dialect distinction with examples: the Bulu, Ewondo, Eton and Mangisa dialects all belong to the Beti-Fang language (Mini-Atlas).
**Application:** Complete a table: name of the language, family, main region, ISO code.
**Assessment:** Each student gives an oral presentation of Tupuri, indicating family and region.
teacher.freedom: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.
teacher.tips: The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas (2013) distinguishes about 280 living languages in Cameroon. The exact number varies according to the criteria (SIL: 274, Ethnologue: 279). Value all the languages cited.

student.intro: Cameroon is one of the richest nations in the world in languages — the linguistic Mini-Atlas lists about 280! In this lesson, you discover the place of Tupuri in this great family.
activities: Look at the Mini-Atlas map and find the area where Tupuri is mainly spoken.
Copy and complete: Tupuri belongs to the ___ family. It is mostly spoken in the ___ region.
According to the Mini-Atlas, how many living languages are there in the Tupuri region? Note down this number.
Survey: ask an adult the name of the language in which they were raised and where it is spoken.
Memorise: **dialect** = an intelligible variant of the same language; **national language** = language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State (ACA LAN).
student.memo: Cameroon has about **280 languages** according to the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas. Tupuri belongs to a Cameroonian language family and has its own dialectal variants. According to the ACA LAN, a national language is the language of an ethnic group that does not extend beyond the borders of one State.

lessons.title: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas
lessons.anelcac: Classification of the languages of Cameroon: linguistic areas, families, ALCAM atlas
objectives: Name the main linguistic areas of Cameroon
Read and interpret an extract from a linguistic atlas (ALCAM / Mini-Atlas)
Classify Tupuri according to its typological criteria
Producing a short text presenting Tupuri

teacher.intro: Lesson: Classification of languages and linguistic atlas. Module: Module I — Cameroonian linguistic diversity.
steps: **Setting the context:** Go back over the definitions. How many language families do students remember?
**Presentation:** The 8 world language families according to Ethnologue (Niger-Kordofanian, Nilo-Saharan, Afro-Asiatic…). Place Cameroonian languages within this whole.
**Explanation:** Show how to find Tupuri in the ALCAM: ISO code, family, location.
**Guided practice:** In pairs, students find 3 languages neighbouring Tupuri and note their ISO codes.
**Production:** 5-line paragraph presenting Tupuri (family, region, speakers, distinctive feature).
teacher.freedom: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.
teacher.tips: The online ALCAM is on the Mozilla Data Collective. The LACAGEO Mini-Atlas covers all the administrative regions with maps and statistics.

student.intro: A linguistic atlas is a specialised map. The ALCAM (Atlas of the Languages of Cameroon) and the LACAGEO Mini-Atlas let you locate Tupuri precisely.
activities: On the Mini-Atlas map, locate Tupuri and note its administrative region.
List 3 languages whose area is adjacent to that of Tupuri.
Classify these 4 languages in a table: Language | Family | Main region.
Write an introductory paragraph about Tupuri with at least 5 pieces of information taken from the atlas.
Memorise: **ISO 639** = international language codes; **ALCAM** = Atlas des Langues du Cameroun.
student.memo: The **ALCAM** and the **LACAGEO Mini-Atlas** list and locate all the national languages of Cameroon. Cameroon has 8 main language families. Tupuri appears there with its family and its location. Knowing how to read a linguistic atlas is reading the history of peoples.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Vowels of Tupuri
lessons.anelcac: AGLC vowels — simple, specific, complex
objectives: Identify the simple vowels of the phonological system of Tupuri
Recognising specific vowels absent from French
Pronouncing vowels correctly in the context of a word
Transcribing words containing vowels according to AGLC

vocabulary.langText: Cɔɓwɛ hee taarag ɓaale ɓɛ gà
vocabulary.langWord: Cɔɓwɛ hee taarag ɓaale ɓɛ gà

vocabulary.langWord: Wããniwa wɔ de kee kɛfdɛr ma had jag depùr de Taynenwa

teacher.intro: Lesson: Tupuri vowels. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write known words in Tupuri on the board and ask which sounds students hear.
**Presentation:** Introduce the AGLC. Write the simple vowels of Tupuri on the board, articulating them clearly.
**Explanation:** Vowels specific to Tupuri that are absent from French (nasal, particular openness…). Listening and repetition exercises.
**Application:** List of 10 words — students underline the vowels and indicate: simple or specific.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 simple words — students transcribe them with the correct vowels.
teacher.freedom: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.
teacher.tips: Use the examples from the platform's ALCAM vocabulary. For each specific vowel, give a memorable key word.

student.intro: Every language has its own sounds. In Tupuri, some vowels do not exist in French. This lesson teaches you to hear, pronounce and write them.
activities: Listen to the recordings of the Tupuri vocabulary and identify the vowels you hear.
Classify the vowels: **Shared with French** | **Specific to Tupuri**.
Transcribe the 5 dictated words, taking care to note each vowel correctly.
Find 3 words in Tupuri for each specific vowel and write them down.
Memorise: **AGLC** = Alphabet Général des Langues Camerounaises, the official reference.
student.memo: The vowel system of **Tupuri** includes simple vowels and specific vowels (e.g. nasalised vowels). They are written using the **AGLC**. Mastery of vowels is the basis of reading and writing in Tupuri.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants
lessons.title: Tupuri consonants and written production
lessons.anelcac: Consonants — simple, specific, complex; written production of vowels and consonants
objectives: Identify the consonant system of Tupuri
Recognising specific consonants absent from French
Articulate consonants correctly in context
Writing words with vowels and consonants correctly notated

vocabulary.langText: Cɔɓwɛ hee taarag ɓaale ɓɛ gà
vocabulary.langWord: Cɔɓwɛ hee taarag ɓaale ɓɛ gà

vocabulary.langText: Wããniwa wɔ de kee kɛfdɛr ma had jag depùr de Taynenwa
vocabulary.langWord: Wããniwa wɔ de kee kɛfdɛr ma had jag depùr de Taynenwa

vocabulary.langText: kããɗa de maŋ ti Lɛ'kããwa de bìi
vocabulary.langWord: kããɗa de maŋ ti Lɛ'kããwa de bìi

teacher.intro: Lesson: Tupuri consonants and written production. Module: Module II — Segmental phonology: vowels and consonants.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the vowels. What is a consonant?
**Presentation:** Table of Tupuri consonants according to the AGLC. Stress the specific consonants (labio-velars, prenasalised, implosives…).
**Explanation:** Articulating difficult consonants: in isolation → syllable → word.
**Application:** Minimal pairs: listening to words that differ only by one consonant.
**Production:** 5 simple sentences in Tupuri with careful consonant transcription.
teacher.freedom: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.
teacher.tips: Implosive and prenasalised consonants are often the most difficult for students who learned to read and write in French. Repeat the listening activities many times.

student.intro: After the vowels, here are the consonants of Tupuri! Some are unique — you will only hear them in Tupuri and in a few neighbouring African languages.
activities: Listen to the minimal pairs and tick the word you hear (e.g. bìlí / pìlí).
Transcribe 5 dictated words, paying attention to the specific consonants.
Find in the vocabulary all the words containing a prenasalised consonant. How many do you find?
Compose 3 simple sentences in Tupuri, each with at least one specific consonant.
Memorise: **minimal pair** = two words identical except for one phoneme.
student.memo: The consonant system of **Tupuri** includes consonants shared with French and specific consonants (implosives, prenasalised, labio-velars…). Writing them according to the **AGLC** is essential for reading and writing.

lessons.title: Definition and functions of tones
lessons.anelcac: Tones — definition, function, presentation; simple tones (high, low, mid)
objectives: Define tone as a distinctive feature of tone languages
Distinguish lexical tone from grammatical tone
Identify the simple tones of Tupuri
Transcribing words with their tones according to AGLC

vocabulary.langText: Á laa wããre jobo gà hase
vocabulary.langWord: Á laa wããre jobo gà hase

vocabulary.langText: ́Bàl maa re coore jar gɔ no
vocabulary.langWord: ́Bàl maa re coore jar gɔ no

vocabulary.langText: Wǔr bày de naage wà ɗa
vocabulary.langWord: Wǔr bày de naage wà ɗa

teacher.intro: Lesson: Definition and function of tones. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Say two Tupuri words that are written the same but have different tones and different meanings.
**Presentation:** Define tone. Present the simple tones of Tupuri and their AGLC diacritics.
**Explanation:** Simple tones: high (´), low (`), mid (¯). Have students repeat each tone.
**Application:** Match recorded words with their tone notation.
**Assessment:** Dictation of 5 words — students note the tones.
teacher.freedom: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.
teacher.tips: Singing the tones helps to memorise them. Use a flute or whistle the tonal melodies.

student.intro: Tupuri is a tonal language: the pitch of your voice changes the meaning of the word! You will learn to hear and write down these tones.
activities: Listen to the pairs of words. For each pair, are the tones the same or different?
Transcribe 5 words with their tones using the AGLC diacritics (´ ` ¯).
Find 2 words in the vocabulary that differ only in tone. What does each one mean?
Sing the tones of a 3-syllable word as High-Low-High, then Low-High-Low. What difference do you hear?
Memorise: high tone = ´ ; low tone = ` ; mid tone = ¯.
student.memo: In **Tupuri**, tone is phonological: it distinguishes words with different meanings. The **simple tones** are high (´), low (`), and sometimes mid (¯). They are written using the **AGLC** diacritics.

lessons.title: Complex tones and tone-marked written production
lessons.anelcac: Complex tones (rising, falling); finding the tone of a word; tonal written production
objectives: Identify the complex tones of Tupuri (rising, falling)
Finding the tone of a word by the isolation method
Transcribing sentences with full tone marking
Producing a short text in Tupuri with correct tones

vocabulary.langText: Á laa wããre jobo gà hase
vocabulary.langWord: Á laa wããre jobo gà hase

vocabulary.langText: ́Bàl maa re coore jar gɔ no
vocabulary.langWord: ́Bàl maa re coore jar gɔ no

vocabulary.langText: Wǔr bày de naage wà ɗa
vocabulary.langWord: Wǔr bày de naage wà ɗa

teacher.intro: Lesson: Complex tones and tonal written production. Module: Module III — Suprasegmental phonology: tones.
steps: **Setting the context:** Recall the simple tones. Announce that some syllables carry two tones in succession.
**Presentation:** Complex tones: falling (̂), rising (̌). Let students hear them and reproduce them.
**Explanation:** Isolation method: say the word with an artificial high tone, then a low one, and listen to which sounds natural.
**Application:** Students find the tone of 10 words in Tupuri using the isolation method.
**Production:** Dialogue of 6 lines in Tupuri with complete tone notation.
teacher.freedom: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.
teacher.tips: The complex falling tone is often the most frequent. Start with it before the rising tone.

student.intro: You know the simple tones. Now for the complex tones of Tupuri — syllables that rise and fall at the same time!
activities: Listen to the recorded words and sort them: Simple tone | Complex tone.
Apply the isolation method to 5 words: say them high, then low, and note the tone you perceive.
Transcribe a dialogue of 4 lines in Tupuri with all the tones marked.
Write a 3-sentence text in Tupuri about an action from your daily life, with tone marking.
Memorise: falling tone = ̂ ; rising tone = ̌.
student.memo: The **complex tones** of **Tupuri** (falling ̂, rising ̌) are melodic movements on a single syllable. The **isolation method** makes it possible to find the tone of an unknown word. A transcription in Tupuri without tones is incomplete.

lessons.title: The noun base and noun classes
lessons.anelcac: NP: constituents, base noun + affixes, noun classes, personal pronouns
objectives: Identify the structure of the noun in Tupuri (base + affixes)
Recognising the noun classes of Tupuri
Form the singular and plural of nouns
Use the personal pronouns corresponding to noun classes

teacher.intro: Lesson: The noun base and noun classes. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a noun in Tupuri in the singular and plural. What changes?
**Presentation:** Noun class: in Bantu and Bantoid languages, nouns are grouped into classes marked by prefixes.
**Explanation:** Main noun classes of Tupuri with singular and plural prefixes.
**Application:** Table: singular → plural for 10 nouns.
**Assessment:** Identify the noun class of 5 nouns.
teacher.freedom: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).
teacher.tips: Start from the nouns that students already use. Noun classes often correspond to semantic categories (humans, animals, objects…).

student.intro: In Tupuri, nouns are organised into **classes**. Each class has its own prefixes for the singular and plural — a much richer system than gender in French!
activities: Using the Tupuri vocabulary, make a table: Singular | Plural | Noun class.
Identify the class prefix in each noun. Highlight it.
Put the following 5 nouns into the plural by changing the prefix according to the class.
Match each noun with its corresponding class pronoun.
Memorise: **noun class** = grammatical category of nouns, marked by prefixes.
student.memo: In **Tupuri**, nouns are organised into **noun classes** marked by prefixes. A change of prefix indicates number. Pronouns, adjectives and verbs agree with the class of the noun.

lessons.title: Noun determiners
lessons.anelcac: Determiners: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives; noun class agreement
objectives: Identify the different types of determiners in Tupuri
Make determiners agree with the noun according to the noun class
Build complex noun phrases
Producing sentences with complete NPs

teacher.intro: Lesson: Noun determiners. Module: Module IV — The noun phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a simple noun phrase. How can it be enriched?
**Presentation:** Determiners in Tupuri: possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives.
**Explanation:** Each determiner agrees with the class of the noun (same class prefix or suffix).
**Application:** Complete noun phrases with the correct determiner according to the class.
**Production:** 5 complex noun phrases (noun + 2 determiners) used in sentences.
teacher.freedom: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Tupuri compared with French.
teacher.tips: Stress class agreement — one of the most distinctive features of Tupuri compared with French.

student.intro: A noun with its determiners becomes much more precise! In Tupuri, determiners agree with the **noun class**.
activities: Complete the NPs with the correct possessive determiner according to the noun class.
Underline the determiners in 5 sentences in Tupuri and identify their type.
Turn each simple noun phrase into a complex noun phrase by adding a demonstrative and a numeral.
Write 5 sentences in Tupuri with at least two determiners per noun phrase.
Memorise: **class agreement** = the determiner changes form according to the noun class.
student.memo: In **Tupuri**, all determiners (possessives, demonstratives, numerals, indefinites, interrogatives) agree with the **noun class** of the noun. A **complex NP** = noun + nominal base + agreeing determiners.

lessons.title: The verb stem and conjugation
lessons.anelcac: VP: constituents, stem, affixes, conjugation, verb tenses
objectives: Identify the verb stem and the conjugation affixes in Tupuri
Conjugate a verb in the main tenses
Analyse the morphological structure of a verb form
Use verb forms correctly in sentences

teacher.intro: Lesson: The verb stem and conjugation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Write a verb form in Tupuri and ask students to identify the stem.
**Presentation:** Break down a verb form: subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes.
**Explanation:** Conjugation paradigm of a common verb in Tupuri in several tenses.
**Application:** Conjugation table: 3 common verbs.
**Assessment:** Translate 5 sentences from French into Tupuri.
teacher.freedom: The TAM system of Tupuri is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.
teacher.tips: The TAM system of Tupuri is often richer than that of French. Start with the most commonly used tenses.

student.intro: The verb is the heart of the sentence in Tupuri. It alone carries tense, aspect, mood and subject! In this lesson, you take apart the verbal mechanics.
activities: Break down 5 verb forms in Tupuri: subject prefix | TAM marker | stem | suffix.
Conjugate the verb 'to eat' in Tupuri in 3 different tenses for all persons.
Identify the tense of 5 sentences in Tupuri and justify your answer.
Translate 3 sentences from French into Tupuri, taking care with the conjugation.
Memorise: **TAM** = Tense-Aspect-Mood; this is what verbal affixes express in Tupuri.
student.memo: In **Tupuri**, a verb form = subject prefix + TAM markers + stem + suffixes. The **TAM** (Tense-Aspect-Mood) system expresses more precise temporal and aspectual nuances than in French.

lessons.title: Verbal moods and negation
lessons.anelcac: Moods: indicative, imperative; negation; written production of simple/complex VP
objectives: Identify and use the main verbal moods of Tupuri
Form the verbal negation
Build simple and complex verb phrases
Producing a text with a variety of moods and aspects

teacher.intro: Lesson: Verbal moods and negation. Module: Module V — The verb phrase.
steps: **Setting the context:** Give an order in Tupuri. Which mood is used?
**Presentation:** Moods in Tupuri: indicative, imperative, and other aspectual moods.
**Explanation:** Formation of the negative in Tupuri: prefix, negative suffix, or particle.
**Application:** Turn 5 affirmative sentences into negative ones and vice versa.
**Production:** 8-sentence text alternating affirmation, negation and imperative.
teacher.freedom: Negation in Tupuri can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.
teacher.tips: Negation in Tupuri can be double (framing the verb) or simple. Show both cases.

student.intro: Giving an order, expressing doubt, denying an action — each nuance has its own form in Tupuri!
activities: Put the 5 given sentences into the negative form.
Turn these 5 statements into imperatives addressed to a friend.
Identify the mood and polarity (affirmative/negative) of each sentence in the text provided.
Write a dialogue of 6 lines including at least 2 imperatives and 2 negations.
Memorise: **mood** = the way of viewing the action; **negation** = grammatical marker denying the action.
student.memo: In **Tupuri**, the main moods are the **indicative** and the **imperative**. **Negation** is marked by a particle or a specific affix. The diversity of moods is an expressive richness of Tupuri.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Tupuri
lessons.title: The simple sentence and its types
lessons.anelcac: Simple, interrogative, negative and imperative sentence; word order
objectives: Analyse the structure of the simple sentence in Tupuri
Distinguish the 4 types of sentences
Mastering the order of constituents
Producing varied simple sentences

teacher.intro: Lesson: The simple sentence and its types. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Tupuri.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a sentence in Tupuri. Who does what?
**Presentation:** Basic constituent order in Tupuri. Compare with French.
**Explanation:** The 4 sentence types from the same basic sentence.
**Application:** Turn declarative sentences into interrogative ones, then into negative ones.
**Production:** 8 varied sentences (2 per type) about school life.
teacher.freedom: Word order in Tupuri may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.
teacher.tips: Word order in Tupuri may differ from French. This is a typological feature, not a mistake.

student.intro: A well-constructed sentence in Tupuri follows precise rules. You learn the types of sentences and word order.
activities: Identify the order of constituents in 5 sentences in Tupuri.
Turn 4 declarative sentences into yes/no questions.
Turn these 4 sentences into negatives.
Write 2 sentences of each type (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative).
Memorise: the basic order in **Tupuri** is typologically stable.
student.memo: The **simple sentence** in **Tupuri** has a characteristic order of constituents. The 4 types (declarative, interrogative, negative, imperative) are formed with specific grammatical markers.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module VI — The sentence in Tupuri
lessons.title: Logical connectors and the complex sentence
lessons.anelcac: Logical connectors, complex sentence, coordination, subordination; written production
objectives: Identify the logical connectors of Tupuri
Distinguish coordination from subordination
Build complex sentences
Producing a coherent text with syntactic variety

teacher.intro: Lesson: Logical connectors and the complex sentence. Module: Module VI — The sentence in Tupuri.
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a short story in Tupuri. Which words link the sentences?
**Presentation:** Connectors in Tupuri: coordinating and subordinating conjunctions.
**Explanation:** Complex sentence by coordination / by subordination. Examples in Tupuri.
**Application:** Link 5 pairs of simple sentences with the appropriate connector.
**Production:** 10-sentence text on 'A day in my village' with 5 different connectors.
teacher.freedom: The connectors of Tupuri often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.
teacher.tips: The connectors of Tupuri often have French equivalents but with different syntactic positions.

student.intro: To tell stories and argue, you need to link your sentences. The **logical connectors** of Tupuri are your tools!
activities: Underline all the connectors in the text provided.
Classify them: Addition | Cause | Consequence | Opposition | Time.
Link 5 pairs of sentences with the most appropriate connector.
Write a text of 8 sentences with at least 4 different connectors.
Memorise: coordination = same level; subordination = one sentence inside another.
student.memo: In **Tupuri**, **logical connectors** make it possible to build coherent **complex sentences**. Varying syntactic structures improves the quality of written and spoken expression.

lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Tupuri
lessons.anelcac: Everyday communication situations: greetings, introductions, polite expressions
objectives: Mastering greeting formulas according to context
Introducing yourself and someone else in Tupuri
Use polite and respectful expressions
Holding a short everyday conversation

teacher.intro: Lesson: Greeting, introducing yourself and interacting in Tupuri. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Two students meet at the market. Act out the scene in French, then ask how to say it in Tupuri.
**Presentation:** Greetings in Tupuri according to the time of day, age and context.
**Explanation:** Formulas of respect towards elders, specific to Tupuri culture.
**Role play:** In groups of 2, simulate encounters in various contexts (market, school, ceremony).
**Production:** Dialogue of 10 lines between two people of different generations.
teacher.freedom: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.
teacher.tips: Greeting rules reflect deep cultural values. Value the knowledge of students from families who speak the language.

student.intro: Knowing how to greet in Tupuri means respecting the culture! The greetings change depending on whom you greet and at what time.
activities: Complete the table of Tupuri greetings: Time | Formula | Expected response.
Play role A: greeting an elder at the morning market.
Make up a dialogue of 8 lines between a child and their grandfather.
Note down 3 Tupuri politeness formulas with no direct equivalent in French.
Memorise the morning and evening greeting formulas, and those for elders, in Tupuri.
student.memo: **Greetings** in **Tupuri** vary according to the time of day, status and social context. They reflect the community's values of respect and solidarity.

lessons.title: Express everyday needs and actions
lessons.anelcac: Real-life situations: shopping, requests for help, travelling, daily activities
objectives: Express everyday needs in Tupuri
Describe daily activities
Use vocabulary for places and actions of everyday life
Producing a descriptive text on a typical day

teacher.intro: Lesson: Expressing everyday needs and actions. Module: Module VII — Everyday life (Level 1).
steps: **Setting the context:** Images of scenes from daily life — market, field, school, home. How can they be described in Tupuri?
**Presentation:** Thematic vocabulary: food, travel, household activities.
**Simulation:** Market scene: buyer and seller in Tupuri.
**Application:** Describe your day in Tupuri (from waking up to going to bed).
**Production:** 10-sentence text: 'My day in Tupuri'.
teacher.freedom: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.
teacher.tips: Everyday vocabulary is the most motivating. Link the ALCAM words to real situations.

student.intro: You know how to greet people. Now you are going to manage in everyday situations in Tupuri: at the market, on the road, at home.
activities: Match each picture of a scene from daily life with the corresponding word or sentence in Tupuri.
Play the role of the seller at the market: answer the requests in Tupuri.
Write 5 sentences describing your morning activities from the time you wake up.
Translate these 5 sentences about daily journeys into Tupuri.
Memorise 10 everyday words in Tupuri with their French translation.
student.memo: The **everyday** vocabulary in **Tupuri** covers food, getting around and household activities. Mastering it allows functional communication in all contexts.

lessons.title: Argue and persuade in Tupuri
lessons.anelcac: Elaborate communication: argumentation, narration, formal speech
objectives: Build a simple argument in Tupuri
Use the expressions of formal speech
Narrating a past event coherently
Delivering a 2-minute oral speech in Tupuri

teacher.intro: Lesson: Arguing and persuading in Tupuri. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Read a proverb in Tupuri. Ask students to explain it and defend it.
**Presentation:** Formulas of formal oral speech in Tupuri: forms of address, opening, closing.
**Explanation:** Structure of an argument: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion.
**Practice:** Debate: for or against the use of Tupuri at school? Each group defends its position.
**Production:** 2-minute speech on a given theme.
teacher.freedom: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.
teacher.tips: Public speaking is highly valued in Cameroonian cultures. Draw on this tradition to motivate the students.

student.intro: In Tupuri cultures, well-spoken words are a force. You learn to argue and persuade with eloquence.
activities: Identify in the text: thesis, arguments, examples.
Prepare 3 arguments to defend the teaching of Tupuri in primary school.
Give an opening speech for a ceremony in Tupuri.
Narration: tell in Tupuri about a memorable event from your school life.
Memorise the opening and closing formulas of a formal speech in Tupuri.
student.memo: **Argumentation** in **Tupuri** follows this pattern: thesis → arguments → examples → conclusion. **Formal speech** follows precise cultural conventions. Mastery of elaborate oral expression is a high-level skill.

lessons.title: Oral literature and advanced written production
lessons.anelcac: Oral literature: proverbs, tales, riddles; long written production
objectives: Analyse the structure of a tale or a riddle in Tupuri
Identify the themes and values conveyed
Writing a short tale following the conventions of the genre
Using oral literature as a teaching resource

teacher.intro: Lesson: Oral literature and advanced written production. Module: Module VIII — Everyday life (Level 2).
steps: **Setting the context:** Tell or play a short tale in Tupuri.
**Presentation:** Genres of oral literature: tales, proverbs, riddles, epics.
**Analysis:** Structure of the tale: initial situation → disruption → events → resolution → moral.
**Application:** Analyse a tale provided, following this structure.
**Production:** Tale of at least 15 lines in Tupuri with an explicit moral.
teacher.freedom: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.
teacher.tips: Oral literature is a threatened cultural treasure. Invite community storytellers if possible.

student.intro: Tupuri tales, proverbs and riddles are literary works in their own right. You will analyse them and you will create your own!
activities: Read the tale provided and identify the 5 stages of its narrative structure.
Identify 3 moral values taught by this tale.
Translate a proverb in Tupuri into French and explain its figurative meaning.
Write a short tale (15 lines) in Tupuri with a moral about work or respect.
Memorise: tale = fictional narrative with an educational purpose; proverb = brief formula of collective wisdom.
student.memo: The **oral literature** of **Tupuri** (tales, proverbs, riddles) transmits the values of the community. The tale has a 5-stage structure. Writing it in Tupuri draws on all the language skills acquired.

lessons.title: Who are the Toupouri (Dziguilao)? Identity, language and territory
lessons.anelcac: Cultural areas, cultural identity, settlement
objectives: Name the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where did they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Toupouri community (Dziguilao): who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Toupouri (Dziguilao) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, once very isolated, today mixed with the Fulani (notably at Guidiguis) and neighbouring the Moundang. • Toupouri is spoken in Chad and, in Cameroon, as far as Touboro, Nkoteng and Mbandjock. • Largely native and endogamous group; men, being more mobile, marry outside more often. • Ancestral land “won at the price of blood”. • Coming from Sudan through Chad, they have lost the link with Sudan but remain very close to the Toupouri of Chad.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their area, the Toupouri, long very isolated, now live alongside the Fulani and Moundang. Having come from Sudan through Chad, with which they live “in absolute fraternity”, they organise their society around the doore (land chiefs), clan notables and maagay initiates. Farming, livestock, bil-bil and pottery are their livelihood, and the cockerel festival, the feo kake, opens the new year every October.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Toupouri (Dziguilao)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
objectives: Identify traditional authorities
Explain how decisions are made
Identifying the rules of deference
lessons.competence: Describe how the Toupouri (Dziguilao) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Toupouri (Dziguilao) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “An important decision has to be made for the whole village of the Toupouri (Dziguilao). Who decides, and how?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The wandoore (in Chad) and the doore lead; the notables are the heads of neighbourhoods and clans (three at Dziguilao); blacksmiths form a caste, the moungouri. • Decisions are taken by consensus between the doore and the notables. • One does not marry within one's own clan; in-laws may joke with each other, by virtue of the alliance. • The maagay lead the initiation. • The woman bows or kneels before handing over water or any object.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)

Decisions are taken by consensus between the doore and the notables. People do not marry within their own clan; in-laws may joke with each other, by virtue of the alliance.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Toupouri (Dziguilao).” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Toupouri (Dziguilao) eat mainly red and yellow millet couscous, bay chèrè and tchenglèrè sauces, baobab leaves, and beef and goat meat. Traditional drinks: bil-bil, arki. These foods are linked to the group's activities and the produce of its environment.

vocabulary.frenchText: “born in the month of the cockerel festival”

lessons.competence: Explain how the Toupouri (Dziguilao) welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born into a Toupouri family (Dziguilao). How will the child be named, and how will they become an adult?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain how the Toupouri (Dziguilao) welcome a child, give them a name and mark their entry into adulthood.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “A child has just been born into a Toupouri family (Dziguilao). How will the child be named, and how will they become an adult?” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • May- marks women's names, Pa- or Wa- men's names. • The name is given according to circumstances, sometimes revealed in a dream; it changes once, at initiation. • Everyone is called by their own name. • The child is a gift from God; the father offers ox trotters for the mother's broth. Death takes one back to the ancestors, who appear through dreams and rituals. • A boy becomes a man around the age of 18 (build, deep voice); a girl around 15, with puberty.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: May- marks women's names, Pa- or Wa- men's. The name is given according to circumstances, sometimes revealed in a dream; it changes once, at initiation. Everyone is addressed by their own name.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Toupouri (Dziguilao)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: traditional economy
objectives: Identify economic activities
Explain the division of tasks
Explain access to land
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Toupouri (Dziguilao). First you need to understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A development project wants to help the Toupouri (Dziguilao). First, we need to understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, livestock, trade. Women: farming, pottery, selling bil-bil. • Land belongs to men; one inherits from one's father or clears one's own space. • Ancestral crafts: clay pots for the home and for sale, hats against the sun.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade. Women: farming, pottery, selling bil-bil. Land belongs to men; one inherits it from one's father or clears one's own plot.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Make a two-column table (men / women) of the activities of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Find out how the Toupouri (Dziguilao) make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify
activities.instruction: Classify the activities in a men / women table.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade. Women: farming, pottery, selling bil-bil. Land belongs to men; one inherits it from one's father or clears one's own plot.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Toupouri (Dziguilao)
lessons.anelcac: Community practices: symbolism, rites, taboos
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
Identify sacred places
Explain the role of taboos
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Toupouri (Dziguilao). Which places and rules must they absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read out: “A visitor arrives among the Toupouri (Dziguilao). What places and rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think about it individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Cults: the feo kake, the cockerel festival, in October at the start of the harvests and of the new year; the festival of the moungouri; the sacred djatobe tree. • Sacred places marked by trees: Djaksiri (sacred land), Koumaijwa, Padde, Guirsay, Bobio, Wersore, Dziguilao. • The child is a gift from God; the father offers cattle trotters for the mother's broth. Death takes one back to the ancestors, who make themselves known through dreams and rituals. • Taboos: talking about initiation, incest; prohibitions: adultery, striking one's elders (uncles, aunts). • Divination with eggs, water, the mirror; there are oracles (halgue, djarkounene).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cults: the feo kake, the rooster festival, held in October at the start of the harvest and of the new year; the moungouri festival; the sacred djatobe tree. Sacred places marked by trees: Djaksiri (sacred land), Koumaijwa, Padde, Guirsay, Bobio, Wersore, Dziguilao.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Toupouri (Dziguilao) (3 places or rules to respect, with the reason for each).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Find out what the Toupouri (Dziguilao) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: Cults: the feo kake, the rooster festival, held in October at the start of the harvest and of the new year; the moungouri festival; the sacred djatobe tree. Sacred places marked by trees: Djaksiri (sacred land), Koumaijwa, Padde, Guirsay, Bobio, Wersore, Dziguilao.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Toupouri
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
Introducing yourself
Counting from 1 to 10

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Toupouri (Dziguilao) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Toupouri (Dziguilao) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in sharing the kola nuts while counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Toupouri (Dziguilao) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read aloud: “You are visiting a Toupouri family (Dziguilao). Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the kola nuts by counting.” Students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Toupouri. • Greeting formulas: Ine/ Lla = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Ndo nayaola/Ndo naawé = morning greeting (one person); Ndo nayaola/Ndo naawé = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Bong, Bogè, Swa’a, Naa, Dwee. • Everyone is called by their own name. • Tchaossala, the oldest ancestor mentioned, was a figure of resistance to the Fulani conquests.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Toupouri are the first steps towards communicating with the Toupouri (Dziguilao). Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Toupouri.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Toupouri are the first steps towards communicating with the Toupouri (Dziguilao). Polite expressions show the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
